question: How many banquets appear in this chapter, who gives them, for whom and for how long?
Why is Vashti's refusal treated as a problem for the whole empire, and what does this reveal about Xerxes' court?
The word דָּת (dat, “law, decree”) reappears throughout the book: what does it govern here, and what can already be seen about the Persian laws that “cannot be repealed”?
Vashti says “no” to an order of the king: in what situations do you need to weigh the cost of refusing a request from someone with power?
What does the text tell us about Mordecai's origin and about Esther's story before she entered the palace?
Why does Mordecai tell Esther not to reveal her people, and what tension does this create for the rest of the narrative?
The word חֵן (chen, “favor, grace”) appears with Esther before Hegai, before everyone and before the king: how does she win this favor, according to the text?
Mordecai uncovers a conspiracy and the fact is only recorded in the chronicles, without reward: how do you deal with the good you do that no one recognizes?
How does Haman react when Mordecai does not bow before him, and what is the disproportion between the offense and the plan?
What half-truths does Haman use to describe the Jews to the king, and why do they convince him?
The word פּוּר (pur, “lot”) explains the name of the feast of Purim: what does it mean that Haman chooses the date of the massacre by lot?
The king and Haman sit down to drink while the city of Susa is “bewildered”: where do you see today decisions made with indifference toward those who will be affected?
What are the signs of mourning of Mordecai and of the Jews in the provinces in the face of the decree?
What does Mordecai mean by “who knows whether you have not come to the kingdom for such a time as this?”, in a book in which the name of God does not appear?
The verb אָבַד (avad, “perish”) appears in Mordecai's warning and in Esther's answer: how does the phrase “if I perish, I perish” change Esther's tone?
Before acting, Esther asks the people to fast for her: whom do you call to be with you before a risky decision?
How does Esther present herself before the king, and why does she postpone her request to a second banquet?
Haman has wealth, sons and honor, but says that “all this gives me no satisfaction”: what does the chapter show about his heart?
The extended שַׁרְבִיט (sharvit, “scepter”) decides between life and death: what weight does this gesture have after what Esther said in 4:11?
A single man who will not bow spoils Haman's joy: what small offenses take up too much room in your heart?
What chain of events, starting with the king's sleepless night, leads to the memory of what Mordecai did?
What irony is there in Haman designing the honor he himself will have to give Mordecai?
The verb נָפַל (nafal, “fall”) appears in the words of Zeresh and the wise men: what do they announce about Haman, and why do they relate it to Mordecai being a Jew?
The turnaround begins in a sleepless night: how do you read the chances and coincidences of your own story?
How does Esther phrase her request, and when does she reveal the name of the enemy?
What does it mean that Haman is hanged on the gallows he prepared for Mordecai, and how does this kind of reversal appear in other biblical texts?
Esther says she and her people have been “sold,” with the verb מָכַר (makar, “sell”): what fact of chapter 3 is she referring to with this word?
Esther openly identifies with her people before the king: at what moment does speaking for others require you to expose yourself?
What passes from Haman's hands to those of Esther and Mordecai in this chapter?
If the first decree cannot be repealed, how does the second decree try to solve the problem, and what does this say about human power?
The טַבַּעַת (tabaat, “signet ring”) passes from Haman to Mordecai: what does it mean to use the same ring to write the opposite of the earlier decree?
Esther asks “how can I bear to see the destruction of my kindred?”: what suffering of others can you not see without acting?
What detail about the plunder does the text repeat three times, and how does it compare with the order of 3:13 and 8:11?
How should we read today the account of the fighting and deaths in this chapter, which the book presents as defense against an extermination already decreed?
The word שִׂמְחָה (simchah, “joy”) marks the days of Purim: what other gestures, besides the feast, does the text link to this joy?
The book commands that the deliverance be remembered “in every generation,” with gifts and gifts to the poor: how do you keep and pass on the memory of what God has done?
How does the book describe Mordecai in its last lines?
Why does the book end by referring to the chronicles of the kings of Media and Persia, and what link does this have with the chronicles of 2:23 and 6:1?
The word רָצָה (ratsah, “please, be accepted”) describes Mordecai among his brothers: what kind of leadership does the verse describe?
Mordecai is remembered for seeking “the good of his people”: how would you use a position of influence for the sake of others?
